Mechanism of the Thermal Decomposition of PEAs
To clarify the poor thermal stability of PEAs derived from EA, their thermal decomposition products were analyzed by DPMS.
Figure 4 shows the DPMS spectra of decomposition products of PEA IId obtained at three different temperatures: 180, 200, and 230 8C.

The DPMS spectra of PEA IId exhibited two main peaks at m/z 217 (AHþ) and $m / z = 1 4 8$(BHþ) assignable to N,N0-divinyl terephthalamide and N-vinyl benzamide, respectively, and also a peak at $m / z = 1 9 2 ~ \mathrm { ( C H ^ { + } ) }$assignable to PEA, indicating the formation of a vinylamide compound with a cyclic monomeric structure.

It has been reported that the thermal decomposition mechanism of aliphatic–aromatic polyesters such as PET and poly(butylene terephthalate) is a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process via a six-membered ring transition state in the ethylene–ester unit, at which carbon–oxygen bond scission takes place to yield carboxyl and vinyl ester end groups<sup>27–30</sup> [Scheme 2(a)].

Montaudo et al.<sup>31</sup> concluded that the primary thermal decomposition process of some aliphatic–aromatic polyamides including poly(ethylene terephthalamide) proceeds via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process accompanying carbon–nitrogen bond scission in the ethylene–amide unit with the formation of thermal decomposition products having amide and N-vinylamide end groups [Scheme 2(b)].
For PEA IId with an amide content of 50 mol %, two thermal decomposition pathways via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process are possible in the ester– ethylene–amide unit [Scheme 2(c)].

The DPMS analysis of PEA suggests strongly that its primary thermal decomposition proceeds via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer reaction accompanying carbon–oxygen bond scission in the ester– ethylene–amide unit via a six-membered ring transition state to form carboxyl and N-vinylamide end groups.

Thermal Stability of PEAs

The thermogravimetric curves of PET and PEAs IIa–IId are shown in Figure $^ { 3 , }$and their $T _ { \mathrm { i } }$and decomposition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { d } } )$values are summarized in Table 1.

$T _ { \mathrm { i } }$and $T _ { \mathrm { d } }$of PEAs IIa–IId decreased significantly with increasing amide content in the polymers, and PEA IId with an amide content of 50 mol % showed a $T _ { \mathrm { i } }$value of 280 8C and a $T _ { \mathrm { d } }$value of $3 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$.
On the other hand, PET had the corresponding temperatures of 366 and 409 ${ } ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C } .$respectively.
Mechanism of the Thermal Decomposition of PEAs
To clarify the poor thermal stability of PEAs derived from EA, their thermal decomposition products were analyzed by DPMS.
Figure 4 shows the DPMS spectra of decomposition products of PEA IId obtained at three different temperatures: 180, 200, and 230 8C.

The DPMS spectra of PEA IId exhibited two main peaks at m/z 217 (AHþ) and $m / z = 1 4 8$(BHþ) assignable to N,N0-divinyl terephthalamide and N-vinyl benzamide, respectively, and also a peak at $m / z = 1 9 2 ~ \mathrm { ( C H ^ { + } ) }$assignable to PEA, indicating the formation of a vinylamide compound with a cyclic monomeric structure.

The DPMS spectra of the decomposition products for PEA IIIb with an amide content of 3 mol % in the different temperature ranges of 310–340, 340– 360, and $3 6 0 { - } 3 8 0 \ { \textdegree } \mathbf { C }$are shown in Figure 5.

In the temperature region of $3 1 0 \mathrm { - } 3 4 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$, the peaks observed at m/z 148 (BHþ), m/z 192 $( \mathrm { C H ^ { + } } ) ,$and $m / z = 5 7 7$were assigned to N-vinyl benzamide, a cyclic monomeric compound of PEA,
and a cyclic trimer of PET, respectively.

It has been reported that the thermal decomposition mechanism of aliphatic–aromatic polyesters such as PET and poly(butylene terephthalate) is a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process via a six-membered ring transition state in the ethylene–ester unit, at which carbon–oxygen bond scission takes place to yield carboxyl and vinyl ester end groups<sup>27–30</sup> [Scheme 2(a)].

Montaudo et al.<sup>31</sup> concluded that the primary thermal decomposition process of some aliphatic–aromatic polyamides including poly(ethylene terephthalamide) proceeds via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process accompanying carbon–nitrogen bond scission in the ethylene–amide unit with the formation of thermal decomposition products having amide and N-vinylamide end groups [Scheme 2(b)].
For PEA IId with an amide content of 50 mol %, two thermal decomposition pathways via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process are possible in the ester– ethylene–amide unit [Scheme 2(c)].

The DPMS analysis of PEA suggests strongly that its primary thermal decomposition proceeds via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer reaction accompanying carbon–oxygen bond scission in the ester– ethylene–amide unit via a six-membered ring transition state to form carboxyl and N-vinylamide end groups.

On the other hand, for the PEAs (EA-modified PETs) containing lower amide contents, at a lower temperature, the ester–ethylene–amide unit in the polymer decomposes exclusively via a hydrogen-transfer process from the carbon next to the amide group.
PEAs prepared in this work were found to decompose at lower temperatures than PET.
For example, PEA IId decomposed at 350 8C, whereas PET did at 409 8C (Table 1).

In the trimer model (I) for PET, all the HOMO electrons were localized on the benzene ring.
On the other hand, in the trimer model (II) for PEA IId, a considerable number of HOMO electrons were distributed on the ester–ethylene–amide unit of the reaction center.

The MO calculation results obtained on the basis of the frontier electron densities for the trimer models could explain well the specific thermal degradation behavior of the PEAs prepared in this work.
